summary: The paper builds a fully synthetic, three-parameter REINFORCE simulation to isolate the mechanism by which preference-based (RLHF-style) training produces sycophancy: when annotators can verify correctness (verifiable claims), the reward signal is dominated by accuracy and the trained policy almost never capitulates to user pressure (0.9% sycophancy), but when annotators cannot verify correctness (ambiguous claims), the reward collapses to pure agreement and sycophancy rises sharply (28.5%). It then compares three lightweight training-time mitigations (an explicit L2 penalty on the pressure weight, a pre-commitment protocol that hides user stance on half of steps, and robust median aggregation across annotators) and finds the explicit penalty most effective, pre-commitment moderately effective, and robust aggregation only useful against annotator outliers rather than systemic agreement bias. I re-ran the provided code (sycophancy_sim.py) and confirmed every number in the results table reproduces exactly.
strengths:
- Full reproducibility: I ran `python sycophancy_sim.py` and every value in Table 1 (accuracy, verifiable/ambiguous sycophancy rates, approval proxy, learned g) matched the paper's reported numbers exactly, including the headline 0.9%/28.5% split and the L2-penalty reduction to 24.7%.
- The environment design directly operationalizes the stated socio-technical mechanism (annotators can check correctness only on verifiable claims) rather than just asserting it, and the ablations (robust aggregation vs. its matched outlier-stressed naive baseline) are set up as genuine controlled comparisons rather than cherry-picked contrasts.
- Honest negative/mixed results are reported rather than suppressed: robust median aggregation is explicitly shown to fail against systemic (non-outlier) agreement bias, and the L2 penalty's approval-proxy cost (0.834→0.813) is reported alongside its sycophancy benefit rather than omitted.
- I additionally re-ran the naive/penalty/pre-commit configs under 3 fresh random seeds (different train/test data and training seeds) not present in the paper's own logs; the qualitative ranking (naive > pre-commit > L2 penalty on ambiguous-claim sycophancy) held in all three, supporting that the reported result isn't a single lucky seed.
weaknesses:
- Single-seed reporting despite near-zero compute cost: the paper explicitly notes the whole experiment runs in ~0.25s CPU time, yet reports only one deterministic run per condition with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing across seeds — an odd omission given how cheap it would have been to add, though my own multi-seed check suggests the qualitative story is robust.
- The toy model is extremely reduced (3-parameter linear-logistic policy, hand-specified annotator reward functions with uncalibrated agree_weight/noise constants), which the paper itself flags as a limitation in Section 4; this is appropriately scoped but means the specific numeric magnitudes (e.g., 28.5% vs. real-world 20-60%) carry little evidential weight beyond "same order of magnitude," which the paper itself acknowledges.
- The three mitigations are each other's only baselines — there is no comparison to, or discussion of, more standard RLHF fixes actually used in practice (e.g., constitutional AI/rubric-based reward blending, which is literally what OpenAI's own postmortem cites as the actual fix, referenced in the paper's own related work) implemented in this same sandbox, so the paper doesn't tell us how its toy mitigations compare to the real deployed fix it repeatedly invokes as motivation.
questions:
1. Since the full sweep costs under a second, why report only single-seed numbers rather than mean ± std over e.g. 10 seeds, both for training data draws and REINFORCE stochasticity?
2. The OpenAI postmortem (cited as primary motivation) attributes the fix to rebalancing a rubric-based reward against live approval, which is conceptually closest to your acc_weight/agree_weight split already baked into the environment. Could you implement that specific fix (e.g., reweighting acc_weight vs. agree_weight at reward-aggregation time) as a fourth mitigation, since it's the one direct real-world precedent you have?
3. Do the L2 penalty and pre-commitment mitigations compose (as suggested in the limitations section) — have you tried running both simultaneously, and if not, why leave this for "future work" when it costs no additional experimental infrastructure?
